result: Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) has shown clinical success in some immunogenic tumors but the majority of patients, even in responsive tumor types like melanoma, do not benefit, and glioblastoma remains largely refractory to ICB therapy.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C8-C9, and C11 collectively establish the clinical landscape of ICB therapy based on established knowledge and clinical observations. These claims accurately represent the current state of ICB efficacy across different tumor types, with particular emphasis on the limited success in glioblastoma.

result: The glioblastoma immune microenvironment is highly immunosuppressive, containing tumor-associated macrophages, tumor-infiltrating dendritic cells, and regulatory T cells that are heterogeneous in ontogeny, spatial distribution, and functionality, leading to defects in anti-tumor T-cell responses.
evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C32, C42, and C69 describe the immunosuppressive nature of the GBM microenvironment based on established knowledge. These claims provide a coherent characterization of the immune landscape in glioblastoma that is well-supported by the literature.

result: Growth and therapy resistance of GBM tumors is mediated by stem-like cells whose tumor-propagating nature is fully regulated by neurodevelopmental transcription factors including POU3F2, SOX2, SALL2, and OLIG2.
evaluation: Claims C14-C16 are supported by citation to Suvà et al., 2014. The claims describe an established mechanism of GBM tumor biology with appropriate attribution to prior work.

result: GBM tumors exhibit molecular heterogeneity with at least three subtypes (TCGA-PN, TCGA-CL, TCGA-MES) that associate with specific genetic alterations and can be further subdivided into four cellular states (MES-like, AC-like, OPC-like, NPC-like), with different subtypes found within the same tumor and dynamic changes over time or in response to therapy.
evaluation: Claims C19-C27 describe GBM tumor heterogeneity based on multiple cited studies (Verhaak et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2017; Sottoriva et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2014; Neftel et al., 2019). The claims accurately represent established findings about GBM molecular classification and cellular states.

result: Non-genetic heterogeneity in GBM is determined by proximity to blood vessels, with mTOR activity upregulated in cells closest to vessels, conferring superior invasive and migratory capabilities and therapy resistance.
evaluation: Claims C28-C30 are supported by citation to Kumar et al., 2019. The claims describe a spatial mechanism of heterogeneity with functional consequences, though C30 involves some inference from the cited work.

result: Intracranial tumors cause entrapment of T cells in bone marrow due to loss of surface S1P1, and reversal of this deficiency enables enhanced T cell migration into GBM tumors.
evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are supported by citation to Chongsathidkiet et al., 2018. The claims describe a specific mechanism of T cell dysfunction in intracranial tumors with therapeutic implications.

result: Thymic involution in GBM tumor-bearers results in diminished T-cell production and reduced availability of T cells for anti-GBM immunity.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by citation to Andaloussi et al., 2008. The claims describe a systemic effect of GBM on T cell availability.

result: Exhausted T cells are enriched in GBM tumors, with tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes more often co-expressing PD-1, LAG3, and TIM-3 than peripheral blood cells, and only triple-positive cells show impaired function while single-positive cells do not.
evaluation: Claims C38-C41 are supported by citations to Woroniecka et al., 2018b and Davidson et al., 2019. The claims describe a specific phenotype of T cell exhaustion in GBM with functional implications based on checkpoint molecule co-expression.

result: Neoadjuvant immunotherapy with anti-PD-1 followed by surgery and adjuvant treatment significantly improved overall survival and progression-free survival in resectable glioblastoma compared to adjuvant treatment alone, with evidence of intratumoral immunomodulatory effects including increased interferon response, chemokine production, and TIL activity.
evaluation: Claims C46-C51 describe clinical trial results supported by multiple citations (Liu et al., 2016; O'Donnell et al., 2019; Cloughesy et al., 2019; Schalper et al., 2019). The claims represent a major advance in GBM immunotherapy with consistent findings from independent studies using different anti-PD-1 antibodies.

result: In preclinical models, anti-PD-1 efficacy is boosted by concurrent administration of chemotherapy, radiation therapy, other immune checkpoint blocking antibodies, cancer cell-directed immunotoxins, and nanocarriers that improve shuttling across the blood-brain barrier.
evaluation: Claims C52-C56 describe combination therapy approaches in preclinical models, each supported by individual citations (Park et al., 2019; Rajani et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2019; Chandramohan et al., 2019; Galstyan et al., 2019). The claims represent promising preclinical strategies for enhancing ICB efficacy.

result: Oncolytic virotherapy with polio-rhinovirus chimera achieved 21% long-term survivors (2-3 years) in clinical trials, and DNX-2401 resulted in 20% of patients surviving >3 years with three patients showing ≥95% tumor reduction, likely due to direct oncolytic effects followed by immune-mediated responses.
evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by citations to Desjardins et al., 2018 and Lang et al., 2018. The claims describe promising clinical outcomes from virotherapy approaches, though C63 involves mechanistic inference.

result: The number and type of immune cells in GBM microenvironment is associated with genetic alterations: TILs are enriched in TCGA-MES tumors with NF1/RB1 mutations but depleted in TCGA-CL, EGFR-amplified, and PTEN-deleted tumors; IDH-wt status associates with higher TIL infiltration and PD-L1 expression while IDH mutations result in reduced IFNγ signature and CD8+/CD4+ cells.
evaluation: Claims C73-C79 are supported by citations to Rutledge et al., 2013; Berghoff et al., 2017; Kohanbash et al., 2017; Luoto et al., 2018. The claims establish important correlations between tumor genetics and immune infiltration patterns.

result: IDH-mutant tumors contain fewer macrophages with more pro-inflammatory M1-like activation, possibly contributing to longer survival; macrophages and neutrophils are increased in TCGA-MES tumors with enrichment of both M1 and M2 genes; computational analysis grouped GBM into three immune subgroups: negative (TCGA-PN, low immune cells), humoral (TCGA-MES, high B-cells/CD4+ T-cells), and cellular-like (TCGA-CL, high macrophages).
evaluation: Claims C81-C88 are supported by citations to Poon et al., 2019; Luoto et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2017. The claims describe complex relationships between tumor genetics, macrophage phenotypes, and immune composition, though C82 involves speculation about survival mechanisms.

result: Despite immunologically different tumor microenvironments in TCGA subtypes, no association was found with ICB responsiveness; instead, non-responders have more PTEN mutations associated with immunosuppressive signatures while responders are enriched in MAPK pathway alterations, illustrating that ICB responsiveness is more complex than mere presence of immune cells.
evaluation: Claims C89-C93 are supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2019. The claims represent an important finding that challenges assumptions about the relationship between immune infiltration and ICB response, identifying specific genetic predictors of response.

result: Radiation therapy induces hypoxia leading to increased CXCL12 production and recruitment of CXCR4/CXCR7-positive bone marrow-derived cells that differentiate into tumor-promoting macrophages mediating vasculogenesis and recurrence; blockade of CXCL12/CXCR7 delays recurrence in preclinical models, and a Phase I/II trial with CXCR4 inhibitor plerixafor (MERT strategy) improved local control of recurrence in newly diagnosed GBM patients.
evaluation: Claims C94-C100 are supported by citations to Tabatabai et al., 2006; Kioi et al., 2010; Tseng et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2014; Walters et al., 2014; Thomas et al., 2019. The claims describe a mechanistic cascade from radiation-induced hypoxia to clinical intervention with strong preclinical and clinical evidence.

result: Temozolomide action depends on immunomodulatory properties; it induces lymphopenia which can be harnessed therapeutically, with lymphoablative doses increasing tumor antigen-specific immune responses in GBM patients and mice, mechanistically through compensatory homeostatic cytokines reducing T-cell activation threshold and inducing proliferation.
evaluation: Claims C103-C107 are supported by citations to Karachi et al., 2018; Sampson et al., 2011; Batich et al., 2017; Sanchez-Perez et al., 2013. The claims describe a counterintuitive therapeutic mechanism, though C107 involves mechanistic speculation.

result: Dexamethasone treatment is associated with lower overall survival in recurrent GBM patients, most likely due to immunomodulatory effects of steroids, with treated patients containing fewer lymphocytes but more potentially suppressive myeloid cells in blood.
evaluation: Claims C108-C110 are supported by citations to Wong et al., 2015 and Chitadze et al., 2017. The claims describe an important clinical consideration regarding standard supportive care that may negatively impact immunotherapy outcomes.

result: TAMs in GBM can be derived from tissue-resident macrophage pools; single-cell RNA sequencing revealed diversity of brain macrophages with parenchymal microglia differing from border-region macrophages; TAMs in GBM are partly derived from embryonic microglia and can be distinguished from monocyte-derived macrophages via lineage tracing, with the GBM microenvironment instructing distinct transcriptional landscapes including differential expression of genes for IL-1 signaling, chemokines, inflammatory cytokines, and antigen presentation.
evaluation: Claims C112-C118 are supported by citations to Movahedi and Van Ginderachter, 2016; Laviron and Boissonnas, 2019; Van Hove et al., 2019; Bowman et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2017. The claims describe important advances in understanding TAM heterogeneity and ontogeny in GBM.

result: In glioblastomas, monocyte-derived macrophages are enriched in tumor core while microglia-derived TAMs are at the periphery; live 2-photon microscopy showed monocyte-derived cells are small and motile while microglia are large sessile cells with continuously extending/retracting processes; these distinct populations have been confirmed in human GBM.
evaluation: Claims C122-C124 are supported by citations to Chen et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019a; Müller et al., 2017; Darmanis et al., 2017. The claims describe spatial and morphological distinctions between TAM populations with validation in human tumors.

result: Cancer cell- and host cell-derived osteopontin mediates macrophage infiltration through integrin αvβ5 interaction and instructs pro-tumoral phenotype; AHR drives CCR2 expression for monocyte recruitment; in PTEN-deficient models, enhanced LOX production attracts macrophages via β1 integrin-PYK2 pathway which subsequently promote tumor growth via SPP1.
evaluation: Claims C126-C129 are supported by citations to Wei et al., 2019; Takenaka et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019b. The claims describe multiple molecular mechanisms governing macrophage recruitment to GBM tumors.

result: GBM-secreted IL-6 induces immunosuppressive PD-L1+ myeloid cells in periphery; CyTOF analysis shows elevated MDSC but not Treg in circulation; MDSC presence in mouse GBM associates with reduced TILs and induces regulatory B cells; TAM-produced CCL2 recruits CCR2+ MDSC and CCR4+ Treg, correlating with reduced survival; CCR2 antagonist sensitizes resistant murine gliomas to ICB.
evaluation: Claims C130-C136 are supported by citations to Lamano et al., 2019; Alban et al., 2018; Raychaudhuri et al., 2015; Lee-Chang et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2016; Flores-Toro et al., 2020. The claims describe the role of MDSC in GBM immunosuppression and a therapeutic strategy targeting their recruitment.

result: Increased FOXP3+ Treg are found in higher-grade brain tumors including glioblastoma, but correlation with decreased survival has been very moderate at best; nevertheless, Treg-directed therapies like anti-GITR or anti-LAP antibodies have shown promise in mouse GBM models.
evaluation: Claims C139-C141 are supported by citations to El Andaloussi and Lesniak, 2007; Jacobs et al., 2010; Yue et al., 2014; Thomas et al., 2015; Miska et al., 2016; Patel et al., 2016; Gabriely et al., 2017. The claims highlight a paradox in Treg biology in GBM with potential therapeutic implications.

result: CCR8 has been identified as a marker specifically expressed in tumor-infiltrating Treg but not peripheral Treg, as part of a conserved tumor-infiltrating Treg transcriptional signature across species and tumor types; CCR8+ Treg are very potent suppressors likely important in creating immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.
evaluation: Claims C146-C147 are supported by citations to Plitas et al., 2016; De Simone et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2017; Magnuson et al., 2018; Barsheshet et al., 2017. The claims identify a specific marker for tumor-infiltrating Treg with therapeutic potential.

result: Nrp1 interaction with Semaphorin 4a stabilizes Treg phenotype in mice, important for suppressing anti-tumor immunity; absence of Nrp1 in Treg leads to loss of suppressive potential and IFNγ production, which annihilates suppressive capacity of neighboring Nrp1+ Treg in murine tumors.
evaluation: Claims C148-C150 are supported by citations to Delgoffe et al., 2013 and Overacre-Delgoffe et al., 2017. The claims describe a molecular mechanism regulating Treg stability and function in tumors.

result: HIF-1α expression in hypoxic tumor-infiltrating Treg decreases intrinsic suppressive activity but is required for Treg migration into mouse GBM tumors; consequently, absence of HIF1α in Treg leads to reduced GBM tumor growth.
evaluation: Claims C151-C153 are supported by citation to Miska et al., 2019. The claims describe a dual role for HIF-1α in Treg function with therapeutic implications.

result: At least three types of conventional DCs (cDCs) plus pDCs are present in tumor microenvironments; cDC1 are rare cells that migrate to tumor-draining lymph nodes for cross-presentation to CD8+ T cells and are attracted by NK cell-secreted Flt3L, CCL5, and XCL1; cDC2 are more abundant, drive CD4+ T cell responses and initiate Th17 responses, but their full potential may only be unleashed without Treg.
evaluation: Claims C154-C159 are supported by citations to Laoui et al., 2016; Roberts et al., 2016; Zilionis et al., 2019; Broz et al., 2014; Böttcher et al., 2018; Barry et al., 2018; Binnewies et al., 2019. The claims describe DC heterogeneity and function in tumors based on studies in non-GBM tumor types.

result: CCR2+ Lin- hematopoietic stem cells can differentiate into cross-presenting DCs in mouse GBM tumors that can be isolated for vaccination to induce anti-tumor immunity and potentiate ICB effects; increasing intratumoral CD103+ cDC1 through Flt3L administration or TLR3 agonist activation magnifies response of mouse glioblastomas to ICB.
evaluation: Claims C163-C167 are supported by citations to Flores et al., 2018; Miao et al., 2018; Garzon-Muvdi et al., 2018. The claims describe strategies to enhance DC-mediated anti-tumor immunity in GBM.

result: Fibrinogen-like Protein 2 (FGL2), predominantly secreted by cancer cells, interferes with induction of immunostimulatory DCs by interfering with GM-CSF signaling, blunting CD103+ cDC1 differentiation and consequently lowering CD8+ T-cell response.
evaluation: Claims C168-C169 are supported by citation to Yan et al., 2019. The claims describe a tumor-derived mechanism for suppressing DC differentiation and function.

result: Nanoparticle delivery systems can cross the blood-brain barrier: solid lipid nanoparticles deliver siRNAs to mouse GBM after low-dose irradiation; LinTT1 peptide targets p32 for GBM-directed nanoparticles; nanoscale immunoconjugates on poly(β-L-malic acid) scaffold with anti-CTLA-4 or anti-PD-1 enable systemic BBB delivery and local brain anti-tumor immune activation.
evaluation: Claims C170-C172 are supported by citations to Erel-Akbaba et al., 2019; Säälik et al., 2019; Galstyan et al., 2019. The claims describe innovative delivery technologies for overcoming the BBB challenge in GBM therapy.

result: Brain-penetrating CSF1R inhibitor repolarized TAMs into more anti-tumoral phenotype reducing GBM progression in mice; blocking anti-CD47 antibody mobilizes phagocytic capacity of both monocyte-derived and microglial TAMs in mouse GBM models.
evaluation: Claims C173-C174 are supported by citations to Pyonteck et al., 2013 and Hutter et al., 2019. The claims describe therapeutic strategies targeting macrophage function in GBM.

result: The inherently heterogeneous nature of glioblastoma and establishment of an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment could be responsible for ICB failure, with heterogeneity strongly undermining therapy efficacy due to likely presence of cancer cell clones able to escape.
evaluation: Claims C12-C13 and C31 represent hypotheses and inferences about mechanisms of ICB resistance. While the heterogeneity and immunosuppression are well-documented, the causal link to ICB failure is speculative and not directly demonstrated in the cited work.

result: Future single-cell RNA-sequencing will allow identification of multiple TAM subsets in glioblastoma.
evaluation: Claim C125 is a prediction about future research based on findings in lung tumors. While reasonable, this represents speculation about what future studies will reveal rather than a current finding.
